title: Introduction to CSS
subtitle: Bring web pages to life with styling
description: Learn what CSS is, how it works with HTML, how to write CSS rules, and how to style your first web page.

blocks.title: 1. What Is CSS?
blocks.text: CSS stands for Cascading Style Sheets. It is the language used to control how HTML elements look on a web page. HTML describes the structure and meaning of content, while CSS controls its presentation. For example, HTML can create a heading, paragraph, button, or navigation menu, while CSS can change their colors, sizes, spacing, borders, and layout. Without CSS, a page can still contain meaningful content, but it usually lacks the visual design expected of a modern website. CSS is not a programming language like JavaScript. It is a stylesheet language that describes presentation rules. A browser reads the HTML, applies the CSS rules that match its elements, and displays the resulting page.

blocks.title: 2. Why Do Websites Need CSS?
blocks.text: CSS helps developers create consistent, readable, attractive, and responsive interfaces. It allows you to separate content from presentation, which makes websites easier to maintain. Imagine a website with twenty pages and the same blue heading on every page. If the color is written separately inside every heading, changing it becomes repetitive. A shared stylesheet can define the heading style once and apply it wherever the rule matches. CSS can also help interfaces adapt to different screen sizes, improve visual hierarchy, and provide feedback when users interact with buttons or links. However, good CSS is not only about decoration. Readability, accessibility, maintainability, and predictable behavior are equally important.

blocks.title: 4. Understanding a CSS Rule
blocks.text: A basic CSS rule contains a selector followed by a declaration block. The selector identifies which HTML elements the browser should target. Inside the braces, each declaration contains a property and a value separated by a colon. A semicolon usually ends each declaration. For example, h1 { color: purple; } targets h1 elements and sets their text color to purple. Here, h1 is the selector, color is the property, and purple is the value. The braces surround the declaration block. A selector can match one element, several elements, or elements that meet a more specific condition. Correct punctuation matters: missing braces, colons, or quotation marks in the wrong places can prevent code from working as intended.

blocks.output: The heading is purple, the paragraph is slate-colored, and the button has a purple background with white text.

blocks.title: 6. Meet the Three Common Selector Types
blocks.text: An element selector targets HTML elements by tag name, such as p or h1. A class selector starts with a period and targets elements whose class attribute contains that class name, such as .card. A class can be reused on multiple elements. An ID selector starts with a hash symbol and targets an element with a matching id attribute, such as #main-title. An ID should be unique within a page. Classes are generally useful for reusable styling, while IDs are useful for identifying a particular element. Remember that the selector in CSS must match the class or ID in HTML. Writing .notice in CSS does not target an element with id="notice"; that element requires #notice.

blocks.title: 8. Three Ways to Add CSS
blocks.text:
There are three common ways to apply CSS. Inline CSS uses a style attribute directly on an HTML element, such as

Hello

. Internal CSS uses a style element inside the HTML document's head. External CSS stores the rules in a separate file, commonly named styles.css, and connects it using a link element such as . External CSS is usually the best choice for multi-page websites because styles can be shared and maintained in one place. Internal CSS can be useful for a single page or a small demonstration. Inline CSS can be convenient for a quick isolated example, but using it extensively makes styling harder to maintain. These methods can interact, and the final result depends on the CSS cascade, specificity, source order, and other rules.

blocks.title: 10. How an External Stylesheet Works
blocks.text: In a real project, you might keep index.html and styles.css as two separate files in the same folder. In the HTML head, write <link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">. In styles.css, write body { font-family: Arial, sans-serif; } and h1 { color: royalblue; }. The browser requests the stylesheet and applies its rules when the file is found and loads successfully. The href path must match the actual file location and name. If the stylesheet is inside a folder called css, the path might instead be css/styles.css. An external stylesheet does not automatically work if the path is wrong, the file is missing, or the request fails. Keep the HTML responsible for structure and the CSS responsible for presentation whenever practical.

blocks.title: 11. CSS Properties You Should Know First
blocks.text: The color property changes text color, while background-color changes an element's background. The font-size property controls text size, and font-family specifies preferred fonts. The margin property creates space outside an element's border, while padding creates space between its content and border. The border property adds an edge around an element, and border-radius can round its corners. The width property sets an element's width, subject to layout rules and constraints. CSS supports different units, including px for CSS pixels, percent values relative to a containing context in many properties, and rem values relative to the root element's font size. Choose units according to the design goal instead of using one unit for every situation.

blocks.title: 13. What Does Cascading Mean?
blocks.text: The word cascading describes how the browser resolves competing CSS declarations. When multiple rules target the same property on the same element, the browser considers factors such as importance, selector specificity, and source order. A more specific selector can beat a less specific selector even if the less specific rule appears later. When declarations have the same relevant priority and specificity, a later declaration can override an earlier one. Inherited properties, such as color in many situations, may pass from a parent element to its children when the children do not have their own winning value. Not every property is inherited. Understanding the cascade helps you explain why a style appears different from what you expected, instead of adding random declarations until the page looks right.

blocks.title: 15. Professional CSS Habits
blocks.text: Write readable CSS and use meaningful class names such as .profile-card or .primary-button. Keep repeated styles in reusable rules instead of copying the same declarations into many places. Format declarations consistently, and remove rules that are no longer needed. Check your page at different screen sizes instead of assuming it will look correct on every device. Maintain sufficient contrast between text and backgrounds, and do not rely on color alone to communicate important information. CSS can improve usability, but styling alone does not guarantee accessibility. Semantic HTML, keyboard support, clear content, and appropriate focus indicators also matter. Finally, test changes in the browser and use its developer tools to inspect which rules are being applied when a style does not behave as expected.

blocks.title: Knowledge Check 1
blocks.question: What is the primary purpose of CSS in a web page?
options: To define the presentation and visual styling of HTML elements
To store user passwords in a database
To replace HTML as the structure of every web page
blocks.explanation: CSS controls presentation, including colors, typography, spacing, borders, and layout. HTML provides the document's structure and meaning.
blocks.hint: Think about which technology controls how a page looks.

blocks.title: Knowledge Check 2
blocks.question: Which part of this rule is the selector? h2 { color: blue; }
blocks.explanation: The selector is h2. It identifies the heading elements that the rule targets.
blocks.hint: The selector appears before the opening curly brace.

blocks.title: Knowledge Check 3
blocks.question: Which CSS declaration correctly changes text color to red?
blocks.explanation: The correct CSS syntax is property: value;. The property is color and its value is red.
blocks.hint: Use the standard CSS property for foreground text color, followed by a colon.

blocks.title: Knowledge Check 4
blocks.question: Which selector targets every HTML element with class="notice"?
blocks.explanation: A class selector starts with a period. The selector .notice targets elements whose class list includes notice.
blocks.hint: A period identifies a class selector; a hash identifies an ID selector.

blocks.title: Knowledge Check 5
blocks.question: Which HTML element connects an external CSS file in the document head?
blocks.explanation: A link element with rel="stylesheet" and the correct href connects an external CSS stylesheet.
blocks.hint: Look for the HTML element used to link external resources.

blocks.title: Knowledge Check 6
blocks.question: What is an important advantage of external CSS on a multi-page website?
options: It lets multiple pages share and maintain the same styles
It guarantees that every style overrides all other styles
It automatically makes the site accessible
blocks.explanation: A shared stylesheet can apply consistent styles across pages and makes site-wide changes easier to maintain.
blocks.hint: Consider how a single stylesheet can be reused by many pages.

blocks.title: Knowledge Check 7
blocks.question: What does padding control?
options: The space between an element's content and its border
The space outside an element's border only
The color of an element's text
The order in which HTML elements are downloaded
blocks.explanation: Padding creates space inside an element, between its content and its border. Margin creates space outside the border.
blocks.hint: Picture the space inside a card surrounding its text.

blocks.title: Knowledge Check 8
blocks.question: A paragraph matches both the p selector and the .notice selector. Both rules set color, and neither uses !important. Which statement is generally correct?
options: The p selector always wins because it names an HTML element
The browser randomly chooses one color
The class selector is more specific and normally wins over the element selector
The rule written first always wins
blocks.explanation: A class selector has greater specificity than an element selector, so its color declaration normally wins in this situation.
blocks.hint: Compare the specificity of a class selector with an element selector.
